<reason>Both sides fought a tight, well-shaped debate, but B (PRO) held the cleaner comparative path. B's core frame — the seller was paid once at ownership prices and, absent inheritance, keeps both the money and the goods — was never dislodged; A's counter (ongoing hosting/rights costs) was asserted but never developed into a reason the whole entitlement should die. B's firebreak against A's load-bearing resale-collapse objection (death is involuntary, unrepeatable, one estate, non-duplicating; "nobody prices off mortality") was concrete and A's reply reduced to a degree claim about friction — which B then turned effectively in closing: A's own words ("it's the friction, not the principle") concede the principle and leave only convenience, while the motion itself supplies unschedulable friction. A's best route, the subscription-flight dilemma, was genuinely sharp and B's "heirs lose nothing" answer gave A material to weigh certain retroactive cost against contingent benefit; but A overclaimed it as a "full concession," and B plausibly answered that the prediction is A's assertion and that visible rent/buy tiers already exist. On retroactivity, B gave an actual principle (non-enforcement of adhesion terms contradicting the seller's own headline representation) plus a stopping point, which was a direct answer rather than a dodge. Meanwhile B's pressure question about the daughter with 900 ebooks exposed the thinness of A's consumer-law alternative, and A's honest answer ("she inherits a licence that ended") left B's "invitation to lose politely" landing hard. A's "next of kin" drafting objection was real but under-pressed after B conceded an estate-based framing. Two clipped A turns are an added execution cost, costing A the end of its opening and its promised third-way ("platform access entitlements") answer to B's dilemma.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's turn of A's friction admission: A conceded the paperback inheritance chain was tolerable because of physical friction, and B converted that into "inheritance is right in principle — death is the friction," combined with the pressure question that reduced A's consumer-protection remedy to a claim the heir cannot value against a company owing her nothing.</best_rebuttal>
